issues.description: DELETE /admin/users/:id has no authentication or admin authorization middleware, so anyone can delete any user.
Sales report endpoint only requires a logged-in user, with no role check, so any customer can read business-sensitive sales data.
Async login handler has no try/catch, so a rejection from login() (or a missing req.body) becomes an unhandled rejection and the request may hang (Express 4).
Email and password from req.body are passed to login() without validation of presence or type, and there is no rate limiting or lockout, which allows brute-force and NoSQL/type-injection attempts.
Raw card data from the client request body is passed to placeOrder without validation, which raises PCI-DSS exposure and trusts unvalidated input; use a payment provider token instead.
Async order handler has no error handling, so failures in placeOrder cause unhandled rejections and hung requests, and the cart is not validated.
The from/to query parameters are passed to salesReport without validation, and the async handler has no error handling, risking injection, bad input, and unhandled rejections.
The id param is not validated and the async handler has no error handling; deleteUser failures cause unhandled rejections and there is no audit logging of the destructive action.
The Authorization header is passed directly to verifyToken, which must handle a missing header and the 'Bearer ' prefix; the catch also swallows all errors without logging.
SQL injection: the email is concatenated directly into the query string instead of using a parameterized query.
MD5 is a fast, broken hash that is unsuitable for password storage; use bcrypt, scrypt, or argon2 with per-user salts.
Hash comparison with !== is not constant-time and may leak timing information; use crypto.timingSafeEqual (or the password hashing library's compare function).
Returning early when the user does not exist skips the hash computation, creating a timing difference that enables user enumeration.
expiresIn given a bare number is interpreted as seconds by jsonwebtoken, so sessionTtlMinutes would yield a much shorter expiry than intended; convert to seconds or use a string like `${n}m`.
No explicit signing algorithm is specified in jwt.sign, and jwt.verify at line 25 does not restrict the allowed algorithms; pin the algorithm (e.g., HS256).
jwt.verify is called without an algorithms option, which allows algorithm confusion; restrict to the expected algorithm.
The cart-full check runs before looking for an existing SKU, so incrementing the quantity of an item already in a full cart is wrongly rejected.
item.quantity is never validated, so negative, zero, fractional, NaN or huge values can corrupt quantities and totals (e.g. a negative quantity yields a negative total).

The caller-supplied item, including priceCents, is copied into the cart unvalidated, so a client-controlled price can be tampered with; the price should be looked up server-side by SKU and checked as a non-negative integer.
Spreading the item copies all arbitrary properties into the cart line (mass assignment); whitelist sku, priceCents and quantity instead.

cartTotal does no validation or overflow protection, so invalid priceCents or quantity values produce NaN or unsafe-integer totals, and the integer-cents guarantee in the header comment is not enforced.
If connection.query throws, release() on line 12 is never called, leaking the pooled connection and eventually exhausting the pool; wrap in try/finally.
Acquiring a client for every single statement via pool.connect() is unnecessary overhead; pool.query() handles acquire/release automatically and safely.

Pool is created without an 'error' event handler, so an idle client error will emit an unhandled 'error' event and can crash the process; also no pool limits or timeouts (max, connectionTimeoutMillis, idleTimeoutMillis) are configured.
query() accepts raw SQL strings with no guard or documentation requiring parameterized usage, making it easy for callers to introduce SQL injection through string concatenation.

Check-then-update race condition (TOCTOU): stock is read in a separate query from the update, so concurrent reservations can oversell; use a single atomic conditional UPDATE (WHERE quantity >= $1) or a transaction with row locking.
The UPDATE query promise is not awaited, so the function returns success before the decrement completes and any database error becomes an unhandled rejection, leaving stock unchanged or inconsistent.
No validation of quantity (could be negative, zero, non-integer, or NaN), so a negative value would increase stock and bypass the availability check.
Generic Error with an interpolated SKU makes it hard for callers to distinguish insufficient stock programmatically; use a custom error type and avoid echoing raw input in messages.
stockLevel returns 0 for unknown SKUs, conflating a nonexistent SKU with out-of-stock, which hides invalid input.
user.name is interpolated into HTML without escaping, allowing HTML injection or phishing content in emails (XSS-style injection).
Empty catch block silently swallows email send errors, so failures are never logged, retried, or reported to the caller.
Currency is hardcoded to "EUR" instead of using the order's currency, which could display incorrect amounts to customers.
formatCurrency argument order (currency, amount) is unconventional and unverified; order.total is used without validation and may be undefined or malformed.
No plain-text alternative body is provided and the subject is generic with no order identifier; user.email is not validated before sending.
The code imports a stub mailer (mailer-stub.js) in what appears to be production code, meaning emails may never actually be sent.
No input validation for user or order parameters; null or undefined values would throw before the try block, giving inconsistent error handling.
Off-by-one loop condition `i <= cart.items.length` accesses an undefined item on the last iteration, causing a TypeError after stock for all real items was already reserved.
Stock is reserved with no rollback if a later reservation or the card charge fails, leaking inventory reservations.
The card is charged with no idempotency key, so retries can double-charge, and there is no refund if the later DB insert fails.
Total is computed server-side from the cart object passed in by the caller, which may be client-controlled and not validated against authoritative prices or quantities.
The order insert is not in a transaction with the stock reservation and charge, so a failure here leaves a charged payment with no order record.
Tax is calculated and returned but not included in the charged total or persisted in the order, so the amount charged may not match what is reported.
A failure in the user lookup or email sending after the charge and insert will throw and make placeOrder appear to fail even though the order was completed.
No validation of userId, cart (e.g. empty, non-positive or non-integer quantities), or card input, and no authorization check that the caller owns userId.
Floating-point multiplication with config.taxRate can introduce rounding inconsistencies, and orderTax does not guard against invalid input.
Logs the full card number and CVC in plaintext, violating PCI DSS and exposing sensitive card data in logs.
No validation of card or amountEuros (type, NaN, negative, zero, non-finite), so invalid or malicious amounts could be sent to the provider.
The provider charge call has no error handling and no idempotency key, so network retries could cause duplicate charges and raw provider errors may leak to callers.
The raw card object (including number and CVC) is passed to the provider rather than a tokenized payment method, increasing PCI scope.
Math.round(amountEuros * 100) can suffer from floating-point errors (e.g. 1.005*100); amounts should be handled as integer cents or with a decimal library.
Empty catch block swallows all refund errors without logging or handling.
refundCharge returns true even when the refund failed, falsely reporting success and potentially leaving customers unrefunded.
chargeId is not validated and there is no idempotency handling or authorization check for refunds.
SQL injection: `from` and `to` are concatenated directly into the query string instead of using parameterized queries.
Empty catch block silently swallows database errors, hiding failures and making debugging impossible.
Returning an empty array on failure makes errors indistinguishable from a legitimately empty report, potentially yielding misleading sales data.
No validation of `from` and `to` inputs (type, date format, range order), and no authorization check despite the report being staff-only.
BETWEEN with a date-only `to` value excludes orders created later that day, and GROUP BY on an alias is not portable across databases.
orderCount has no error handling, inconsistent with salesReport, and COUNT(*) may be returned as a string/bigint so Number conversion could lose precision on very large counts.
SQL injection: the email is concatenated directly into the query string instead of using a parameterized query (e.g. WHERE email = $1 with [email]).
deleteUser performs no authorization or ownership check, so any caller can delete any user account if this function is exposed without upstream access control.
Database calls have no error handling or input validation, so failures propagate as raw database errors to callers.
Off-by-one error: slice(start, start + pageSize - 1) returns only pageSize-1 items per page; the end index should be start + pageSize.
No validation of page or pageSize (zero, negative, non-integer, or NaN values) which can produce a negative start index and incorrect slices.
No validation that amountCents is a finite number, so invalid input yields output like 'NaN EUR'; also negative or non-integer cents are not handled explicitly.
Email regex is overly permissive (accepts consecutive dots, leading/trailing dots in domain, no length limit) and may give false positives for validation.
